specPoints.text: understand the concept of a reaction mechanism
understand the link between bond polarity and the type of reaction mechanism a compound will undergo

primer.text: Mechanisms are electron choreography, drawn with curly arrows - two heads for pairs, one for lone electrons. This note teaches the notation, then uses bond polarity as the fortune-teller: non-polar mixtures turn radical, polar bonds breed electrophiles and nucleophiles for addition and substitution.

lessons.title: Curly arrows: the grammar of mechanisms
lessons.opening: Equations count the molecules; mechanisms choreograph the electrons. Double-headed curly arrows move electron pairs, single-headed fish-hooks move lone electrons, and three reaction families - addition, substitution, elimination - carry the notation.
keyPoints: Reaction mechanisms show how a reaction actually takes place, unlike equations which show amounts and stoichiometry.
A double-headed curly arrow carries an electron pair from its source to its destination.
Single-headed fish-hook arrows carry one electron each, marking homolytic splits, radical termination and propagation.
Curly arrows feature in addition, substitution and elimination mechanisms.

low.restatement: The arrow is a traffic sign for electrons: two heads means a pair moves, one head means a single electron moves - and every mechanism step is drawn with them.
low.analogy: Two-lane versus single-lane roads: pairs travel the dual carriageway (double-headed), solitary radicals take the single-track (fish-hook).
low.examPointer: Never mix arrow types in one step: pair arrows for heterolytic chemistry, fish-hooks only for radical steps.

medium.restatement: Electron-pair movement begins from a bond or a lone pair and lands where the new bond forms; radical chemistry moves single electrons during fission, propagation and termination. The three families named reuse the same notation across organic chemistry.
medium.analogy: Ballroom dancers (pairs) versus solo street dancers (single electrons): the choreography arrows differ accordingly.
medium.examPointer: An arrow's tail starts AT the electron source (bond or lone pair) - tails never start from atoms or charges.

check.stem: What do reaction mechanisms show that equations do not?

options.text: How the reaction actually takes place, step by step
options.explanation: Mechanisms choreograph electron movement; equations only count species.

options.text: The overall stoichiometry in detail
options.explanation: Equations already provide stoichiometry.

options.text: The enthalpy change of the reaction
options.explanation: Enthalpy is thermochemistry, not mechanism.

options.text: The masses of the products
options.explanation: Mass data belongs to equations and calculations.

options.text: The movement of a pair of electrons
options.explanation: Two heads, two electrons - the pair convention of heterolytic chemistry.

options.text: The movement of a single electron
options.explanation: Single electrons use the fish-hook arrow.

options.text: The movement of an atom
options.explanation: Atoms are not moved by curly arrows; electrons are.

options.text: A reversible reaction step
options.explanation: Reversibility uses half-arrows in equations, not curly arrows.

check.stem: A single-headed fish-hook arrow is used when

options.text: A covalent bond splits homolytically, giving two radicals
options.explanation: One electron goes to each fragment, so each movement is single-headed.

options.text: A nucleophile donates a lone pair to a cation
options.explanation: Lone-pair donation moves a pair, needing a double-headed arrow.

options.text: Water splits a halogenoalkane
options.explanation: Hydrolysis mechanisms use pair arrows.

options.text: An electrophile adds to an alkene
options.explanation: Electrophilic addition moves electron pairs.

options.text: Two radicals combining their unpaired electrons into a covalent bond
options.explanation: The fish-hook arrows bring the two single electrons together into one bond.

options.text: A bond splitting evenly into two radicals
options.explanation: That is homolytic fission, the initiation-side step.

options.text: A radical reacting with a stable compound to propagate
options.explanation: That is propagation, not termination.

options.text: A pair of electrons attacking a positive centre
options.explanation: Pair chemistry, not radical termination.

check.stem: Which three reaction families use curly-arrow mechanisms?

options.text: Addition, substitution and elimination
options.explanation: The note names exactly these three as the curly-arrow families.

options.text: Combustion, neutralisation and precipitation
options.explanation: None of these uses organic curly-arrow notation here.

options.text: Redox, hydrolysis and esterification
options.explanation: Not the named trio at this level.

options.text: Polymerisation, cracking and distillation
options.explanation: Distillation is not even a reaction.

check.stem: State what a double-headed curly arrow shows.
check.modelAnswer: An electron pair travels from the arrow's tail (a bond or lone pair) to its head, where the new bond or ion forms.

check.stem: Name the arrow type that moves one electron.
Explain why homolytic fission needs single-headed arrows.
check.modelAnswer: The bond's two electrons split one to each fragment, so each electron's movement is drawn with its own single-headed arrow.

check.stem: A mechanism step shows a methyl radical's unpaired electron joining a chlorine atom's unpaired electron. Draw the arrow type and name the step.
check.modelAnswer: Two fish-hook arrows (one from each unpaired electron) converge into the new C-Cl bond; this is radical termination.

lessons.title: Bond polarity points to the mechanism
lessons.opening: Polarity is the fortune-teller of mechanisms: all-non-polar bonds hint at homolytic fission and radical substitution, while a clearly polar bond invites heterolytic fission and the electrophile-nucleophile cast. Ethane versus ethene with HBr show both readings.
keyPoints: Bond polarity can suggest the likely mechanism of a reaction.
Ethane with chlorine: all bonds non-polar or barely polar, so homolytic fission and free radical substitution are suggested.
HBr added to ethene: the polar H-Br bond breaks heterolytically, and the alkene's double bond attracts the electrophile, suggesting electrophilic addition.
Heterolytic fission creates an electron-deficient electrophile and an electron-rich nucleophile.

low.restatement: No polarity to exploit means radicals; a polar bond splits into a positive electrophile and a negative nucleophile, and the alkene's electron-rich double bond waves the electrophile in.
low.analogy: A neutral crowd disperses evenly (radicals); a magnet pair snaps into plus and minus (heterolytic ions) - the mechanism follows the magnetism.
low.examPointer: Justify mechanism choice with TWO polarity sentences: bond polarity of reagent, then the attraction target (double bond or d+ carbon).

medium.restatement: Heterolytic fission of a polar bond gives the electrophile (electron deficient) and nucleophile (electron rich); homolytic fission of non-polar bonds gives radicals. The substrate's feature - electron-rich pi bond or d+ carbon - selects which species attacks first.
medium.analogy: A see-saw with a weight (polar bond) tips riders into defined roles; an unweighted see-saw leaves both riders free-ranging (radicals).
medium.examPointer: Name the mechanism fully: 'free radical substitution' and 'electrophilic addition' - partial names cost the mark.

check.stem: The reaction C2H6 + Cl2 -> C2H5Cl + HCl is likely to proceed by

options.text: Free radical substitution, since all bonds are non-polar or barely polar
options.explanation: No polarity exists to drive heterolytic fission, so radicals form homolytically.

options.text: Electrophilic addition, since chlorine is an electrophile
options.explanation: There is no double bond to add across in ethane.

options.text: Nucleophilic substitution, since chloride is a nucleophile
options.explanation: No polar C-X bond exists in ethane for nucleophilic attack.

options.text: Elimination, since HCl is eliminated
options.explanation: The pattern is substitution of H by Cl, not elimination.

check.stem: Heterolytic fission of a covalent bond produces

options.text: A positive electron-deficient ion and a negative electron-rich ion
options.explanation: The pair goes to one fragment, leaving the other electron-poor.

options.text: Two neutral radicals each carrying one electron
options.explanation: That is homolytic fission's outcome.

options.text: Two positive ions sharing the electron pair
options.explanation: The pair lands on only one fragment.

options.text: No charged species at all
options.explanation: Heterolytic fission is defined by ion formation.

check.stem: In ethene reacting with HBr, the electrophile is attracted to

options.text: The electron-rich carbon-carbon double bond
options.explanation: The pi electrons draw the electron-seeking electrophile.

options.text: The hydrogen atoms of ethene
options.explanation: Hydrogens are not the electron-rich site.

options.text: The bromide ion formed
options.explanation: Bromide is the nucleophile-side product.

options.text: The reaction solvent
options.explanation: Solvent is not the reacting target.

check.stem: Why does the polarity of H-Br suggest heterolytic fission?

options.text: The bond already carries d+ H and d- Br, so the pair drifts to bromine as it breaks
options.explanation: Existing polarity pre-figures the unequal split of the bonding pair.

options.text: Non-polar bonds always split heterolytically
options.explanation: Non-polar bonds split homolytically.

options.text: Bromine is a radical former with hydrogen
options.explanation: No radical chemistry is implied by the polar bond.

options.text: Hydrogen repels electrons completely
options.explanation: Polarity is partial charge, not full repulsion.

check.stem: A nucleophile is best described as

options.text: An electron-rich species attracted to positive or electron-deficient centres
options.explanation: Nucleophiles donate electron pairs to d+ targets.

options.text: An electron-deficient species seeking electrons
options.explanation: That is the electrophile.

options.text: A neutral radical seeking bonds
options.explanation: Radicals are the homolytic cast, not nucleophiles.

options.text: Any negative ion whatsoever
options.explanation: Definition runs on electron richness and attraction, not charge alone.

check.stem: State the likely mechanism when all bonds in a reaction mixture are non-polar.
check.modelAnswer: Homolytic fission and free radical substitution.

check.stem: Name the species created by heterolytic fission.
check.modelAnswer: A positive electrophile (electron deficient) and a negative nucleophile (electron rich).

check.stem: Explain why ethene reacts with HBr by electrophilic addition.
check.modelAnswer: H-Br is polar, suggesting heterolytic fission into H+ (electrophile) and Br-; the electron-rich double bond of ethene attracts the electrophile, so electrophilic addition follows.

check.stem: Predict, with polarity reasoning, whether methane chlorination or ethene bromination is the radical reaction.
check.modelAnswer: Methane chlorination is the radical one: all its bonds are non-polar, so homolytic fission and radical substitution apply; ethene bromination instead runs electrophilic addition through the polarised Br-Br approaching the pi bond.

glossary.definition: The notation showing electron movement in mechanisms; double-headed for pairs, single-headed for single electrons.
Bond breaking in which each fragment takes one electron, forming two radicals.
Bond breaking in which one fragment takes the electron pair, forming an electrophile and a nucleophile.
An electron-deficient species attracted to electron-rich centres such as double bonds.

figures.caption: During this propagation step, the unpaired electron from chlorine and one of the electrons from the C-H bond react together to form a new covalent bond and the other electron from the C-H bond moves to form a methyl radical
During this step of an addition reaction, the lone pair from the bromide ion reacts with the positive carbocation to form a new covalent bond
